--- unit: "C" chapter: "11" lecture: "11b" metadata-files: - ../../_slide-settings.yml format: revealjs: theme: default --- ::: {.my-title} # [Statistical Methods]{.blue} Categorical Moderation ::: {.my-grey} [Unit {{< meta unit >}} | Chapter {{< meta chapter >}}]{}
[Lecture {{< meta lecture >}}]{} ::: ::: {.my-attrib} {{< meta attribution >}} ::: ![](../../img/growth_curve_357EDD.png){.absolute bottom=30 right=0 width="400"} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: # Review ## Review of Last Lecture - We learned about **moderation** via **interaction terms** - The interaction effect is the slope of the product $x_1 x_2$ + This allows the slope of $x_1$ to *depend on* the value of $x_2$ + (and vice versa, slope of $x_2$ on value of $x_1$) - We focused on interactions between *continuous* variables + There were infinite slopes (one for each value of $x_2$) + So we chose to "spotlight" just a few possible slopes ## Example moderation questions {.fs70} **Continuous-by-Continuous Interaction** - Does the effect of `duration` on `expenditure` depend on `intensity`? ::: {.fragment} **Continuous-by-Categorical Interaction** - Does the effect of `duration` on `expenditure` depend on `sex`? ::: ::: {.fragment} **Categorical-by-Categorical Interaction** - Does the effect of `program` on `expenditure` depend on `sex`? ::: ::: {.fragment} **Higher-Order Interaction** - Does the interaction of `duration` and `intensity` depend on `sex`? ::: # Binary-by-Continuous ## Motivation - Can we interact categorical and continuous predictors? + Yes! In fact, in some ways, it is even easier than before + Instead of infinite slopes, we have **one slope per category** ::: {.pv4} - Let's moderate a continuous predictor by a binary variable + *Does the effect of `duration` differ by `sex`?* + Perhaps exercise is more "costly" for men or women... ::: ## Adding Interaction Term - If $x_1$ is continuous and $x_2$ is binary, we can dummy code $x_2$ + $c_1=0$ for the reference group ($x_2=$ female) + $c_1=1$ for the non-reference group ($x_2=$ male) - We will then add an interaction term $x_1 c_1$ with its own slope $$\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + b_2 c_1 + b_3 x_1 c_1$$ ::: {.fragment .tc} `formula = expenditure ~ duration * sex` ::: ## Interpreting the Coefficients {.fs70} $$\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + b_2 c_1 + b_3 x_1 c_1$$ - $b_0$ (intercept): the predicted value of $y$ when $x_1=0$ and $c_1=0$ - $b_1$ (simple): the change in $y$ expected for a change of +1 in $x_1$ (at $c_1=0$) - $b_2$ (simple): the difference in $y$ between the two $x_2$ groups (at $x_1=0$) - $b_3$ (interaction): two equivalent definitions + the difference in $b_1$ (i.e., the slope of $x_1$) between the two $x_2$ groups + the difference in $b_2$ (i.e., the difference between the two $x_2$ groups) expected for a change of +1 in $x_1$ ## Rearranging the Formula $$\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + b_2 c_1 + b_3 x_1 c_1$$ ::: {.fragment} $$\hat{y} = b_0 + (b_1 + b_3 c_1) x_1 + b_2 c_1$$ ::: ::: {.fragment} Thus, the slope of $x_1$ (its multiplier) *depends on* the $x_2$ group Also, if there is no interaction ($b_3=0$), then $b_1$ is unchanged ::: ::: {.fragment .pv2} The same is true for the slope of $c_1$ if we rearrange again $$\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + (b_2 + b_3 x_1) c_1$$ ::: ## Interaction and Simple Effects ::: {.cell replace_path='["../../data/",""]'} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) exercise <- read_csv("../../data/exercise.csv") fit <- lm(expenditure ~ duration * sex, data = exercise) model_parameters(fit) ## Parameter | Coefficient | SE | 95% CI | t(896) | p ## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------- ## (Intercept) | 3.33 | 2.73 | [-2.02, 8.69] | 1.22 | 0.222 ## duration | 3.32 | 1.33 | [ 0.70, 5.93] | 2.49 | 0.013 ## sex [male] | 3.57 | 3.91 | [-4.11, 11.25] | 0.91 | 0.362 ## duration × sex [male] | -1.72 | 1.90 | [-5.45, 2.00] | -0.91 | 0.364 ``` ::: - The interaction effect (duration $\times$ sex) is NOT significant - Thus, the effect of `duration` does NOT depend on `sex` ## Predicting energy expenditure {.fs70} $$\hat{y} = 3.33 + 3.32 x_1 + 3.57 c_1 - 1.72 x_1 x_2$$ - **Intercept:** A female participant exercising at 0 duration expends 3.33 units - **Duration Simple Effect:** Each unit of duration will expend another 3.32 units (for females) - **Sex Simple Effect:** Males will expend 3.57 units more than females (at 0 duration) - **Interaction Effect:** The slope of duration will decrease by 1.72 for males, and the male--female difference will decrease by 1.72 for each added unit of duration ::: {.fragment} The average participant (2 duration) expends 9.97 units (female) or 10.1 units (male) $$\text{Female: }\hat{y} = 3.33 + 3.32(2) + 3.57(0) - 1.72(2)(0) = 9.97$$ $$\text{Male: }\hat{y} = 3.33 + 3.32(2) + 3.57(1) - 1.72(2)(1) = 10.10$$ ::: ## Plotting interaction effects ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} #install.packages("marginaleffects") library(modelbased) plot(estimate_relation(fit, by = c("duration", "sex"))) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-3-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: {.footer} You can tell there is not a significant interaction because the lines could be parallel. ::: ## Plotting interaction effects {.fs90} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(estimate_means(fit, by = c("sex", "duration=[sd]")), join_dots = TRUE) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-5-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: {.footer} You can still spotlight `duration` but then you lose some information. ::: ## Simple slopes - What is the slope of `duration` in each `sex` group? ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} estimate_slopes(fit, trend = "duration", by = "sex") ## Estimated Marginal Effects ## ## sex | Slope | SE | 95% CI | t(896) | p ## ------------------------------------------------------ ## female | 3.32 | 1.33 | [ 0.70, 5.93] | 2.49 | 0.013 ## male | 1.59 | 1.35 | [-1.06, 4.24] | 1.18 | 0.240 ## ## Marginal effects estimated for duration ## Type of slope was dY/dX ``` ::: ## Marginal Contrasts - Is the `sex` difference significant at any value of `duration`? + Usually only do this if the interaction is significant ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} estimate_contrasts(fit, contrast = "sex", by = "duration = [sd]") ## Marginal Contrasts Analysis ## ## Level1 | Level2 | duration | Difference | SE | 95% CI | t(896) | p ## ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ## male | female | 1.51 | 0.97 | 1.33 | [-1.63, 3.58] | 0.73 | 0.464 ## male | female | 2.00 | 0.12 | 0.94 | [-1.72, 1.96] | 0.13 | 0.898 ## male | female | 2.50 | -0.73 | 1.33 | [-3.34, 1.87] | -0.55 | 0.580 ## ## Variable predicted: expenditure ## Predictors contrasted: sex ## p-values are uncorrected. ``` ::: ## Reporting Results > We used a linear model to regress the continuous energy expenditure variable on the continuous exercise duration variable, the binary biological sex variable (dummy coded as 0=female, 1=male), and the duration-by-sex interaction. > > The simple slope of duration was significant for females (p=.013) but not for males (p=.240) and the simple slope of sex was not significant at 0 duration (p=.362). The duration-by-sex interaction was not significant (p=.364). ## Dropping the interaction - Unless the interaction was my main research question, I might drop a non-significant interaction and re-estimate the model to get *partial* effects (rather than simple effects) ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit2 <- lm(expenditure ~ duration + sex, data = exercise) model_parameters(fit2) ## Parameter | Coefficient | SE | 95% CI | t(897) | p ## ----------------------------------------------------------------- ## (Intercept) | 5.02 | 2.00 | [ 1.10, 8.95] | 2.51 | 0.012 ## duration | 2.47 | 0.95 | [ 0.60, 4.33] | 2.60 | 0.009 ## sex [male] | 0.12 | 0.94 | [-1.72, 1.96] | 0.13 | 0.899 ``` ::: # Nominal-by-Continuous ## Expanding the equation - The same approach applies for a **nominal** moderator + But needs multiple dummy codes and interaction terms $$\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + b_2 c_1 + b_3 c_2 + b_4 x_1 c_1 + b_5 x_1 c_2$$ ::: {.tc .fragment} `formula = expenditure ~ duration * program` (`program` $\in\{\text{jog, swim, read}\}$ needs 2 dummy codes) ::: ## Interpreting coefficients {.fs60} $$\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x_1 + b_2 c_1 + b_3 c_2 + b_4 x_1 c_1 + b_5 x_1 c_2$$ - $b_0$ (intercept): expected $y$ at $x_1=0$ and $c_1=c_2=0$ (i.e., reference group) - $b_1$ (simple): change in $y$ expected with change of +1 in $x_1$ (in reference group) - $b_2$ (simple): difference in $y$ between reference and $c_1=1$ group (at $x_1=0$) - $b_3$ (simple): difference in $y$ between reference and $c_2=1$ group (at $x_1=0$) - $b_4$ (interaction): two equivalent definitions + difference in $b_1$ (effect of $x_1$) between reference and $c_1=1$ group + change in $b_2$ (effect of $c_1$) expected with change of +1 in $x_1$ - $b_5$ (interaction): two equivalent definitions + difference in $b_1$ (effect of $x_1$) between reference and $c_2=1$ group + change in $b_3$ (effect of $c_2$) expected with change of +1 in $x_1$ ## Running the model {.fs90} - Let's first pick a reference group for `program` + `"read"` may be a good choice as it is a "control" group ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} # reorder the levels to set "read" first (to make it the reference) exercise$program <- factor(exercise$program, levels = c("read", "jog", "swim")) fit3 <- lm(expenditure ~ duration * program, data = exercise) model_parameters(fit3) ## Parameter | Coefficient | SE | 95% CI | t(894) | p ## ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ## (Intercept) | 2.22 | 1.49 | [ -0.70, 5.13] | 1.49 | 0.136 ## duration | -2.96 | 0.71 | [ -4.35, -1.57] | -4.18 | < .001 ## program [jog] | -9.00 | 2.22 | [-13.35, -4.65] | -4.06 | < .001 ## program [swim] | 9.93 | 2.18 | [ 5.66, 14.21] | 4.56 | < .001 ## duration × program [jog] | 10.41 | 1.07 | [ 8.30, 12.51] | 9.71 | < .001 ## duration × program [swim] | 9.83 | 1.05 | [ 7.77, 11.89] | 9.35 | < .001 ``` ::: ## Plotting the interaction ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(estimate_relation(fit3, by = c("duration", "program"))) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-11-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Plotting the interaction {.fs90} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(estimate_means(fit3, by = c("program", "duration=[sd]")), join_dots = TRUE) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-13-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Centering {.fs90} - Do we really care about effects at zero duration? + If not, the simple effects' tests are not interesting - We may prefer to center `duration` instead + Now the simple effects' tests are at the *average* duration ::: {.fs70} ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit4 <- lm(expenditure ~ center(duration) * program, data = exercise) model_parameters(fit4) ## Parameter | Coefficient | SE | 95% CI | t(894) | p ## ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ## (Intercept) | -3.70 | 0.38 | [-4.44, -2.97] | -9.85 | < .001 ## center(duration) | -2.96 | 0.71 | [-4.35, -1.57] | -4.18 | < .001 ## program [jog] | 11.85 | 0.53 | [10.80, 12.89] | 22.29 | < .001 ## program [swim] | 29.62 | 0.53 | [28.57, 30.66] | 55.73 | < .001 ## center(duration) × program [jog] | 10.41 | 1.07 | [ 8.30, 12.51] | 9.71 | < .001 ## center(duration) × program [swim] | 9.83 | 1.05 | [ 7.77, 11.89] | 9.35 | < .001 ``` ::: ::: ## Probing the interaction ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} estimate_slopes(fit4, trend = "duration", by = "program") ## Estimated Marginal Effects ## ## program | Slope | SE | 95% CI | t(894) | p ## --------------------------------------------------------- ## read | -2.96 | 0.71 | [-4.35, -1.57] | -4.18 | < .001 ## jog | 7.45 | 0.81 | [ 5.87, 9.03] | 9.25 | < .001 ## swim | 6.87 | 0.78 | [ 5.35, 8.40] | 8.84 | < .001 ## ## Marginal effects estimated for duration ## Type of slope was dY/dX ``` ::: ## Probing the interaction ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} estimate_contrasts(fit4, contrast = "program", by = "duration = [sd]", p_adjust = "holm") ## Marginal Contrasts Analysis ## ## Level1 | Level2 | duration | Difference | SE | 95% CI | t(894) | p ## --------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ## jog | read | 1.51 | 6.70 | 0.75 | [ 5.22, 8.18] | 8.89 | < .001 ## swim | read | 1.51 | 24.76 | 0.75 | [23.29, 26.22] | 33.12 | < .001 ## swim | jog | 1.51 | 18.06 | 0.76 | [16.57, 19.54] | 23.91 | < .001 ## jog | read | 2.00 | 11.84 | 0.53 | [10.80, 12.88] | 22.28 | < .001 ## swim | read | 2.00 | 29.61 | 0.53 | [28.57, 30.66] | 55.73 | < .001 ## swim | jog | 2.00 | 17.77 | 0.53 | [16.73, 18.81] | 33.46 | < .001 ## jog | read | 2.50 | 16.99 | 0.75 | [15.53, 18.46] | 22.73 | < .001 ## swim | read | 2.50 | 34.48 | 0.74 | [33.03, 35.93] | 46.63 | < .001 ## swim | jog | 2.50 | 17.48 | 0.78 | [15.96, 19.01] | 22.45 | < .001 ## ## Variable predicted: expenditure ## Predictors contrasted: program ## p-value adjustment method: Holm (1979) ``` ::: # Categorical-by-Categorical ## Expanding the equation - We can also interact two categorical variables - We need two sets of dummy codes (e.g., $[c_1]$ and $[d_1,d_2]$) $$\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 c_1 + b_2 d_1 + b_3 d_2 + b_4 c_1 d_1 + b_5 c_1 d_2$$ ::: {.tc .fragment} `expenditure ~ sex + program + sex:program` ::: ## Simple and interaction effects {.fs70} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit5 <- lm(expenditure ~ sex * program, data = exercise) model_parameters(fit5) ## Parameter | Coefficient | SE | 95% CI | t(894) | p ## ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ## (Intercept) | -3.62 | 0.53 | [-4.66, -2.58] | -6.80 | < .001 ## sex [male] | -0.34 | 0.75 | [-1.81, 1.14] | -0.45 | 0.656 ## program [jog] | 7.91 | 0.75 | [ 6.43, 9.39] | 10.51 | < .001 ## program [swim] | 32.74 | 0.75 | [31.26, 34.22] | 43.49 | < .001 ## sex [male] × program [jog] | 7.82 | 1.06 | [ 5.73, 9.91] | 7.35 | < .001 ## sex [male] × program [swim] | -6.26 | 1.06 | [-8.35, -4.17] | -5.88 | < .001 ``` ::: - **Intercept:** estimates expenditure for females in read - **Male:** male -- female in read - **Jog:** jog -- read for females - **Swim:** swim -- read for females - **Male x Jog:** (a) male -- female in jog, (b) jog -- read for males - **Male x Swim:** (a) male -- female in swim, (b) swim -- read for males ## Estimating means ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} estimate_means(fit5, by = c("sex", "program")) ## Estimated Marginal Means ## ## sex | program | Mean | SE | 95% CI | t(894) ## --------------------------------------------------------- ## female | read | -3.62 | 0.53 | [-4.66, -2.58] | -6.80 ## male | read | -3.96 | 0.53 | [-5.00, -2.91] | -7.43 ## female | jog | 4.29 | 0.53 | [ 3.24, 5.33] | 8.06 ## male | jog | 11.77 | 0.53 | [10.73, 12.82] | 22.12 ## female | swim | 29.12 | 0.53 | [28.07, 30.16] | 54.71 ## male | swim | 22.52 | 0.53 | [21.48, 23.57] | 42.32 ## ## Variable predicted: expenditure ## Predictors modulated: sex, program ``` ::: ## Estimating contrasts {.fs90} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} estimate_contrasts(fit5, contrast = "sex", by = "program") ## Marginal Contrasts Analysis ## ## Level1 | Level2 | program | Difference | SE | 95% CI | t(894) | p ## -------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ## male | female | read | -0.34 | 0.75 | [-1.81, 1.14] | -0.45 | 0.656 ## male | female | jog | 7.48 | 0.75 | [ 6.01, 8.96] | 9.94 | < .001 ## male | female | swim | -6.60 | 0.75 | [-8.07, -5.12] | -8.76 | < .001 ## ## Variable predicted: expenditure ## Predictors contrasted: sex ## p-values are uncorrected. ``` ::: ## Estimating contrasts {.fs90} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} estimate_contrasts(fit5, contrast = "program", by = "sex") ## Marginal Contrasts Analysis ## ## Level1 | Level2 | sex | Difference | SE | 95% CI | t(894) | p ## ------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ## jog | read | female | 7.91 | 0.75 | [ 6.43, 9.39] | 10.51 | < .001 ## swim | read | female | 32.74 | 0.75 | [31.26, 34.22] | 43.49 | < .001 ## swim | jog | female | 24.83 | 0.75 | [23.35, 26.31] | 32.99 | < .001 ## jog | read | male | 15.73 | 0.75 | [14.25, 17.20] | 20.89 | < .001 ## swim | read | male | 26.48 | 0.75 | [25.00, 27.96] | 35.18 | < .001 ## swim | jog | male | 10.75 | 0.75 | [ 9.27, 12.23] | 14.28 | < .001 ## ## Variable predicted: expenditure ## Predictors contrasted: program ## p-values are uncorrected. ``` ::: ## Plotting the interaction {.fs90} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(estimate_means(fit5, by = c("sex", "program")), join_dots = TRUE) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-23-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Plotting the interaction {.fs90} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(estimate_means(fit5, by = c("program", "sex")), join_dots = TRUE) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-25-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: # Three-Way Interactions ## When two-way isn't enough {.fs70} ::: {.columns .pv4} ::: {.column width="60%"} - So far, each interaction has let *one* effect depend on *one* moderator ::: {.fragment .mt1} - But a two-way interaction can itself depend on a third variable + Does the sex-by-program difference hold at every exercise duration? + Perhaps program matters more for men only in longer sessions ::: ::: {.fragment .mt1} - This is a [three-way interaction]{.b .blue}: moderation of a moderation ::: ::: ::: {.column .tc .pv4 width="40%"} {{< lif "../../icons/funnel.json" trigger=hover colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}} ::: ::: ## Expanding the equation {.fs70} - With three predictors, every combination gets a term - For a continuous $x$ and two dummy codes $c_1$ and $d_1$: $$\hat{y} = b_0 + b_1 x + b_2 c_1 + b_3 d_1 + b_4 x c_1 + b_5 x d_1 + b_6 c_1 d_1 + b_7 x c_1 d_1$$ - Three main effects, three two-way interactions, one three-way interaction ::: {.tc .fragment} `expenditure ~ duration * sex * program` ::: ## Fitting the model {.fs90} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} fit6 <- lm(expenditure ~ duration * sex * program, data = exercise) model_parameters(fit6) ## Parameter | Coefficient | SE | 95% CI | t(888) | p ## -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ## (Intercept) | 0.88 | 1.80 | [ -2.64, 4.41] | 0.49 | 0.623 ## duration | -2.24 | 0.86 | [ -3.93, -0.55] | -2.60 | 0.009 ## sex [male] | 2.92 | 2.67 | [ -2.33, 8.16] | 1.09 | 0.275 ## program [jog] | -15.81 | 2.76 | [-21.23, -10.39] | -5.73 | < .001 ## program [swim] | 19.51 | 2.71 | [ 14.20, 24.83] | 7.20 | < .001 ## duration × sex [male] | -1.54 | 1.27 | [ -4.03, 0.96] | -1.21 | 0.227 ## duration × program [jog] | 12.06 | 1.35 | [ 9.40, 14.71] | 8.91 | < .001 ## duration × program [swim] | 6.60 | 1.31 | [ 4.03, 9.17] | 5.04 | < .001 ## sex [male] × program [jog] | 14.98 | 3.98 | [ 7.18, 22.79] | 3.77 | < .001 ## sex [male] × program [swim] | -18.70 | 3.90 | [-26.36, -11.04] | -4.79 | < .001 ## (duration × sex [male]) × program [jog] | -3.91 | 1.92 | [ -7.69, -0.14] | -2.03 | 0.042 ## (duration × sex [male]) × program [swim] | 6.23 | 1.88 | [ 2.54, 9.93] | 3.31 | < .001 ``` ::: ## Reading the output {.fs70} - The coefficient table gets long fast (3 predictors gives 12 terms here) ::: {.fragment .mt1} - Read it [top-down]{.b .blue}, highest-order term first + If the three-way term is significant, the two-way interactions should not be read as *overall* effects + Each lower-order term is now conditional on the others being zero ::: ::: {.fragment .mt1} - In practice, don't interpret this table coefficient-by-coefficient + Probe it with estimated slopes and contrasts instead ::: ## Probing: slopes by both moderators {.fs90} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} estimate_slopes(fit6, trend = "duration", by = c("sex", "program")) ## Estimated Marginal Effects ## ## sex | program | Slope | SE | 95% CI | t(888) | p ## ------------------------------------------------------------------ ## female | read | -2.24 | 0.86 | [-3.93, -0.55] | -2.60 | 0.009 ## male | read | -3.78 | 0.93 | [-5.61, -1.94] | -4.04 | < .001 ## female | jog | 9.81 | 1.04 | [ 7.77, 11.86] | 9.41 | < .001 ## male | jog | 4.36 | 1.00 | [ 2.40, 6.33] | 4.37 | < .001 ## female | swim | 4.36 | 0.99 | [ 2.42, 6.30] | 4.42 | < .001 ## male | swim | 9.06 | 0.98 | [ 7.13, 10.98] | 9.24 | < .001 ## ## Marginal effects estimated for duration ## Type of slope was dY/dX ``` ::: - One duration slope per sex-by-program cell ## Does the sex gap shift with duration? {.fs90} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} estimate_contrasts(fit6, contrast = "sex", by = c("program", "duration = [sd]"), p_adjust = "holm") ## Marginal Contrasts Analysis ## ## Level1 | Level2 | program | duration | Difference | SE | 95% CI | t(888) | p ## -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- ## male | female | read | 1.51 | 0.60 | 0.95 | [ -1.26, 2.46] | 0.63 | > .999 ## male | female | jog | 1.51 | 9.68 | 0.96 | [ 7.79, 11.57] | 10.04 | < .001 ## male | female | swim | 1.51 | -8.71 | 0.95 | [-10.57, -6.85] | -9.19 | < .001 ## male | female | read | 2.00 | -0.16 | 0.67 | [ -1.48, 1.16] | -0.24 | > .999 ## male | female | jog | 2.00 | 6.99 | 0.67 | [ 5.67, 8.31] | 10.38 | < .001 ## male | female | swim | 2.00 | -6.39 | 0.67 | [ -7.70, -5.07] | -9.51 | < .001 ## male | female | read | 2.50 | -0.92 | 0.89 | [ -2.68, 0.83] | -1.03 | 0.907 ## male | female | jog | 2.50 | 4.29 | 1.00 | [ 2.33, 6.25] | 4.29 | < .001 ## male | female | swim | 2.50 | -4.06 | 0.97 | [ -5.98, -2.15] | -4.17 | < .001 ## ## Variable predicted: expenditure ## Predictors contrasted: sex ## p-value adjustment method: Holm (1979) ``` ::: ## Plotting the interaction {.fs90} ::: {.cell} ```{.r .cell-code} plot(estimate_relation(fit6, by = c("duration", "sex", "program"))) ``` ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](b_Slides_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-30-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ## Proceed with caution {.fs70} ::: {.columns .pv4} ::: {.column width="60%"} - Three-way interactions are [expensive]{.b .blue} + They need substantially more power than two-way terms + Cells get small quickly once you cross three variables + Our example is *simulated*, with 150 per cell --- real data is rarely this generous ::: {.fragment .mt1} - They are also easy to over-read + A significant three-way term found post hoc is a prime HARKing risk + Prefer to predict them in advance and preregister ::: ::: {.fragment .mt1} - If you fit one, [plot it]{.b .green} -- the coefficient table alone will rarely tell you what is going on ::: ::: ::: {.column .tc .pv4 width="40%"} {{< lif "../../icons/caution.json" trigger=hover colors=secondary:#2a76dd class=rc >}} ::: :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
